findings.title: Attacker-controlled 32-bit length drives an unbounded heap allocation before any data is read (readBytes)
findings.impact: A peer that can put bytes on the socket (a rogue/compromised broker, or an off-path attacker on a non-TLS connection) forces the client JVM to allocate up to ~2 GB of heap from 5 bytes of wire data, producing OutOfMemoryError and killing the whole JVM, not just the connection. Reached pre-authentication: connection.start server-properties is a field table decoded before any credential is sent.
findings.evidence: readBytes() reads a 32-bit length, widens it unsigned, and its only guard is `if(contentLength < Integer.MAX_VALUE)` before `new byte[(int)contentLength]`. The length is never reconciled with frame-max or with the bytes actually remaining in the stream, and the array is allocated BEFORE in.readFully(buffer) can fail. 0x7FFFFFFE yields a 2147483646-byte allocation from a 5-byte frame. Reachable from readLongstr() (public API, and field-value type 'S') and from field-value type 'x' at line 211.
findings.recommendation: Bound the allocation: reject any contentLength greater than the negotiated frame-max / a configurable max inbound body size, and greater than the bytes actually available in the enclosing stream, throwing MalformedFrameException. If very large values must be supported, read incrementally into a growing buffer with a hard cap rather than pre-sizing from the declared length. The project already carries an inbound frame-max notion (pom.xml references an InboundFrameMax test class), so the limit exists at the frame level and simply is not applied at the value level - ValueReader is a static-helper class with no access to any connection limit, so plumbing one in is the structural part of the fix.

findings.title: Unbounded nesting depth in field-table/field-array decoding causes StackOverflowError
findings.impact: A single small frame drives the decoder thousands of frames deep and throws StackOverflowError. Being an Error, not an IOException/MalformedFrameException, it bypasses the malformed-frame handling this decoder's callers are written around: the connection I/O thread (or a consumer callback thread) dies with an unhandled Error, and each level also leaks a HashMap/ArrayList plus two stream wrappers.
findings.evidence: readFieldValue -> case 'F' -> readTable (line 181/139) and case 'A' -> readArray (line 184/237) recurse with no depth counter and no depth parameter anywhere in the class. A nested table costs 6 bytes per level on the wire (1-byte shortstr length + 'F' + 4-byte length) and a nested array 5 bytes ('A' + 4-byte length), so a default 128 KiB frame reaches >20,000 levels; with a broker-proposed unlimited frame-max the depth is unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Thread a depth argument through readFieldValue/readTable/readArray and throw MalformedFrameException past a small fixed limit (AMQP tables are not meant to nest deeply; 10-16 is generous). Do the same for total element count.

findings.title: Malformed wire input raises an unchecked UnsupportedOperationException instead of MalformedFrameException
findings.impact: A remote peer chooses which exception type the decoder throws. A RuntimeException escapes the IOException/MalformedFrameException handling the frame machinery uses for hostile input, so a protocol-level error surfaces as an unhandled runtime failure on the I/O thread or inside user callbacks instead of a clean connection teardown.
findings.evidence: readBytes() throws `new UnsupportedOperationException("Very long byte vectors and strings not currently supported")` on the else branch of the length check, i.e. on a value supplied by the remote peer. Every other rejection path in this class (line 217) uses MalformedFrameException, which extends IOException.
findings.recommendation: Throw MalformedFrameException (or another IOException) for over-long declared lengths so hostile input stays inside the checked error path.

findings.title: Duplicate field-table keys are silently dropped, first occurrence wins
findings.impact: Header smuggling. A table carrying the same key twice is resolved by this parser as the FIRST value while a peer or middlebox that resolves last-wins (or rejects duplicates) sees a different value for the same message. Any authorization, routing or dedup decision keyed on a header can be made to disagree between the two views, and no error is raised to signal the ambiguity.
findings.evidence: readTable() does `if(!table.containsKey(name)) table.put(name, value);` - a later duplicate is parsed, discarded and never reported. A field table is a set of name/value pairs and AMQP 0-9-1 does not define a resolution order for a repeated name, so each implementation picks its own - which is exactly why silently normalizing it here, rather than rejecting it, creates a cross-parser disagreement an attacker controls.
findings.recommendation: Reject a repeated key with MalformedFrameException, or at minimum make the resolution explicit and logged. Silently discarding attacker-chosen duplicates is the failure mode that creates the parser disagreement.

findings.title: Field names are decoded with lossy UTF-8 replacement, allowing distinct wire keys to collide into one map key
findings.impact: Invalid UTF-8 in a short string never fails; every bad byte becomes U+FFFD. Different byte sequences therefore collapse to the same String, and combined with the first-wins duplicate rule (F-004) an attacker can place a crafted key earlier in the table so that it captures the slot of a legitimate key that arrives later, or shadow a key the application looks up by name.
findings.evidence: readShortstr() returns `new String(b, "utf-8")`, which uses CharsetDecoder REPLACE action; the raw bytes are discarded and there is no validation of the decoded name before it is used as the HashMap key at line 152.
findings.recommendation: Decode with a CharsetDecoder configured with CodingErrorAction.REPORT (or StandardCharsets.UTF_8 plus an explicit validity check) and reject malformed names with MalformedFrameException. Use StandardCharsets.UTF_8 rather than the charset name while there.

findings.title: Timestamp decoding multiplies an attacker-controlled 64-bit value by 1000 with silent overflow
findings.impact: A remote peer picks the sign and magnitude of the resulting Date at will: values above ~9.2e15 ms wrap, so a far-future POSIX second decodes to a date in the past (and vice versa). Application logic that trusts a message timestamp for expiry, ordering, replay windows or audit records can be steered to the wrong side of a comparison.
findings.evidence: readTimestamp() is `new Date(in.readLong()*1000)` - no range check, and the multiplication is plain long arithmetic that wraps silently. AMQP 0-9-1 timestamps are unsigned 64-bit seconds, so the whole upper half of the range is also misread as negative.
findings.recommendation: Use Math.multiplyExact (or an explicit range check) and reject out-of-range timestamps with MalformedFrameException instead of wrapping.

findings.title: Declared table/array length is never reconciled with the enclosing frame, and end-of-table is inferred from available()
findings.impact: A table or array may declare up to 4294967295 bytes inside a frame that is orders of magnitude smaller; the mismatch is only discovered as an EOFException deep inside a nested read, after the nested allocations of F-001/F-002 have already been attempted. Conversely, because the loop terminates on available() == 0 rather than on the declared length being consumed, a table is silently accepted as complete whenever the underlying stream reports no bytes ready - correct only while the frame body is fully buffered in memory, a property this class does not enforce and cannot see.
findings.evidence: readTable() (line 142) and readArray() (line 240) take `unsignedExtend(in.readInt())` straight into TruncatedInputStream with no upper bound, then loop on `while(tableIn.available() > 0)` (lines 148, 244); neither checks afterwards that exactly tableLength bytes were consumed.
findings.recommendation: Validate the declared length against the bytes remaining in the enclosing stream before constructing the TruncatedInputStream, and drive the loop off a remaining-bytes counter, asserting it reaches exactly zero, rather than off available().

findings.title: Manifest is cleanly pinned, but slf4j-api sits on an EOL 1.7.x branch and the build runs on Groovy 2.4.21
findings.impact: No exploitable path found. Flagged because slf4j-api 1.7.36 is the only compile-scope dependency left on an end-of-life branch (everything else - netty 4.2.15, jackson 2.21.3, micrometer 1.17.0, metrics 4.2.39 - is current), and groovy-all 2.4.21 executes at generate-sources time as a build-time supply-chain surface on a line that has been unmaintained for years.
findings.evidence: pom.xml line 58 `<slf4j.version>1.7.36</slf4j.version>` on a non-optional, non-test dependency (line 376); line 81 `<groovy.all.version>2.4.21</groovy.all.version>` injected into groovy-maven-plugin (line 596) to run codegen.py at generate-sources. Positives worth recording: no version ranges, no SNAPSHOT dependencies, no repository/pluginRepository overrides at all, and no plaintext-HTTP resolution URL anywhere in the file.
findings.recommendation: Move slf4j-api to the maintained 2.x line (or record the deliberate decision to stay on 1.7 for consumer compatibility) and move the codegen step onto a maintained Groovy line.

findings.title: readTable returns an immutable map for an empty table and a mutable one otherwise, and the remote peer picks the branch
findings.impact: The mutability of a decoded header table is decided by attacker-supplied bytes. Any caller that decodes headers and then adds to the returned map - a normal thing to do in a consumer or an interceptor - works for every message until a peer sends a zero-length table, at which point Collections.emptyMap() throws UnsupportedOperationException. That is a remotely triggerable crash in application code, reachable at will and easy to miss in testing because the common path is mutable.
findings.evidence: readTable() line 143 `if (tableLength == 0) return Collections.emptyMap();` versus line 145 `Map<String, Object> table = new HashMap<String, Object>();` on the non-empty path. Nothing in the method signature or javadoc tells the caller the return value's mutability varies.
findings.recommendation: Return the same type on both paths - either always a fresh HashMap, or always an unmodifiable wrapper - and state the contract in the javadoc.
